title: 1608: The Spyglass Appears
summary: In 1608 a Dutch spectacle maker named Hans Lipperhey put two lenses in a tube and found that faraway things looked three times closer. Soon other people said they had made one too, and within a year spyglasses were being sold in Paris. In England, Thomas Harriot used one to draw the Moon.

sections.heading: A Letter to The Hague
paragraphs: Imagine the autumn of 1608 in The Hague, the town where the leaders of the young Dutch Republic met. The streets are busy with messengers, soldiers, diplomats and merchants. Inside a government hall, the members of the States General, the national assembly of the Dutch provinces, are working through a pile of letters. One of them, dated 2 October 1608, comes from a spectacle maker in the port town of Middelburg. He asks for something unusual: a patent, which is an official promise that only he may make and sell a new invention for a number of years. The invention, he writes, is an instrument 'for seeing things far away as if they were nearby.'

That letter is the oldest written record of a telescope anywhere in the world. Before it, there are rumors, hints and later stories, but no document that clearly describes a working tube for seeing far. After it, the telescope spreads across Europe so quickly that within about a year people in Paris, Milan, Venice and London are peering through them. In this part we will follow that explosion: the men who claimed the invention, how the first spyglass actually worked, why generals and admirals wanted one desperately, and how one English scientist quietly pointed his at the Moon before almost anyone else.

The man who wrote the letter was Hans Lipperhey, whose name is also often spelled Lippershey. He was born around 1570 in Wesel, a town on the river Rhine in what is now Germany. Like many people in those years, he moved west to the Netherlands, which was booming with trade. He settled in Middelburg in 1594, married that same year, and became a citizen of the province of Zeeland in 1602. He ran a shop where he ground lenses and made spectacles, the eyeglasses we met in the last part.

Middelburg was a good place for such a business. It was a wealthy trading town, a home base for ships of the Dutch East India Company, which had been founded in 1602, and it had plenty of customers who read, wrote, kept accounts and needed help seeing their work. A spectacle maker's shop was full of glass blanks, grinding dishes, polishing powders and finished lenses of many different strengths. In other words, it was exactly the kind of place where someone might pick up two lenses, hold them in a line and discover something surprising.

There is a well-known story that children playing in Lipperhey's shop held two lenses up together, saw a distant church weathervane suddenly look close, and ran to tell him. It is a charming tale, and you will find it in many books, but it is a legend. No document from the time says it happened. What we really know is simpler: by the autumn of 1608 Lipperhey had a working instrument, he believed it was valuable, and he wanted the government to protect his idea.

sections.heading: Rivals at the Door: Metius and the Refused Patent
paragraphs: Lipperhey was not alone for long. On 17 October 1608, only about two weeks after his letter, the States General received a second request for a patent on the same kind of device. It came from Jacob Metius, an instrument maker and lens grinder who lived in Alkmaar, a town in the north of Holland. Metius came from a clever family. His father, Adriaan Anthonisz, was a mathematician, mapmaker, military engineer and mayor of Alkmaar, and his brother, Adriaan Metius, became a well-known geometer and astronomer.

Metius said that he too had made an instrument that could make far-off things look near. He also claimed that he understood the secrets of glassmaking and that, with some government support, he could build an even better one. In other words, he was saying: Lipperhey may have a tube, but I can do more.

The States General now had a problem. If two different men in two different towns had built the same device within a few weeks of each other, how secret could it really be? The officials also noticed how simple the instrument was. Once you knew that it was just two lenses in a tube, almost any skilled spectacle maker could copy it. A patent is only worth something if an idea is new and hard to guess, and this idea was neither. In the end the patent was refused, partly because it was clear that other people already knew about the invention.

Even so, the government did not send Lipperhey away empty-handed. The States General saw that the instrument could be useful to the army, so they hired him to build more of them, and they paid him well. They also asked him for something new: a version for both eyes. Lipperhey made binocular instruments, two tubes joined side by side, which makes him one of the very first makers of binoculars, more than two centuries before the prism binoculars you might use today. Metius received only a small award. According to later accounts, he felt snubbed, kept his own telescope hidden, and in his will asked for his tools and designs to be destroyed so that nobody else could profit from them.

There were more hints that the idea was floating around. The German astronomer Simon Marius later wrote that a Dutchman had tried to sell a spyglass at the great autumn trade fair in Frankfurt in 1608, though the lens was cracked. Several historians think that the basic trick of combining a convex and a concave lens may have been discovered more than once, by craftsmen who did not write anything down. That is why it is fairest to say that the telescope appeared in the Netherlands in 1608, and that Lipperhey's letter is the first record we have of it, rather than to name one single genius as its inventor.

sections.heading: The Janssen Puzzle
paragraphs: If you look up 'who invented the telescope' you will sometimes see a third name: Zacharias Janssen, another spectacle maker in Middelburg, who lived just a few streets from Lipperhey. Some books even say that Janssen built a telescope, and a microscope too, as early as 1590. So why do most historians today doubt this?

The answer lies in when and how the claim was made. Janssen was probably born around 1585, which means that in 1590 he would have been a small child. The story that he invented the telescope did not appear until 1655, about twenty years after his death. In that year a Dutch diplomat named Willem Boreel, who had grown up in Middelburg, tried to find out who had really invented the telescope. Janssen's son, Johannes Zachariassen, gave testimony before a Middelburg magistrate. He said his father had invented the telescope in 1590 and that Lipperhey had stolen the idea.

Johannes's statements, however, did not hang together well. At different times he gave different dates for his father's invention, including 1590 and 1604. Witnesses were trying to remember events from fifty or sixty years earlier, and Boreel may have mixed up the names of spectacle makers he had known as a boy. Records show no clear evidence that Zacharias Janssen worked as a spectacle maker before about 1616. He also had a colorful history: between 1613 and 1619 he was taken to court several times for making counterfeit coins.

A French writer, Pierre Borel, repeated the Janssen claim in a book in 1656, and that is how it spread into many later histories. Modern historians who studied the documents closely, including the telescope historian Albert Van Helden, concluded that Johannes most likely made up or stretched the story, perhaps hoping for fame or money. Sadly, many of Middelburg's old archives were destroyed by bombing in 1940, during the Second World War, so some questions can never be fully settled.

So where does that leave us? The fairest summary is this. Lipperhey made the first known patent request, on 2 October 1608. Metius made a similar request two weeks later. Janssen may possibly have been one of several Middelburg craftsmen experimenting with lenses around the same time, but the claim that he definitely invented the telescope rests on shaky evidence given many years later by his own son.

sections.heading: Inside the First Spyglass
paragraphs: What did the very first telescopes actually look like? Picture a tube a little longer than your forearm, made of paper, leather, wood or thin metal. At the far end sits a convex lens, the kind that bulges outward in the middle, like the lenses in reading glasses for farsighted people. Near your eye sits a concave lens, the kind that is thinner in the middle and thicker at the edges, like the lenses for nearsighted people. Look through the small end at a church tower across town, and the tower seems about three times closer than before.

Here is how it works. The front lens is called the objective. When light from a distant tower passes through it, refraction, the bending of light as it moves from air into glass and out again, bends the rays inward so that they start to come together. If nothing stopped them, they would meet at a point called the focus and form a small upside-down image there. The distance from the lens to that point is the focal length. A weakly curved lens has a long focal length, and a strongly curved lens has a short one.

In this early design, the concave lens is placed a little before the light reaches the focus. It catches the gathering rays and spreads them out again just enough that they enter your eye almost parallel, the way light from a far-off object normally does. Your eye then sees an image that is upright, not upside down, and larger than normal. How much larger depends on the two focal lengths: divide the focal length of the objective by the focal length of the eyepiece, and you get the magnification. A front lens with a focal length of about 30 cm combined with an eyepiece lens of about 10 cm gives about 3 times.

That was roughly the power of Lipperhey's instrument. A three-times spyglass does not sound like much today, when cheap binoculars magnify 8 or 10 times. But imagine never having seen anything bigger than your eyes alone could show. Suddenly the face of a person on the far side of a harbor, the flag on a ship, or the numbers on a distant clock became readable. To people in 1608, it was close to magic.

Why had no one put these two lenses together and written about it during the three hundred years that spectacles had existed? Partly because the right combination is not obvious. You need a weak convex lens and a much stronger concave lens, set at just the right distance apart. Ordinary reading glasses were fairly weak, and strong concave lenses for very nearsighted people were less common. The glass of the time was also often bubbly, greenish and unevenly polished, so many lens pairs simply gave a blurry mess. Early makers learned a useful trick: covering the edge of the front lens with a ring of card or metal so that only the middle part was used. This cut down the blur from badly shaped edges, although it also let in less light.

sections.heading: Eyes for Armies and Navies
paragraphs: To understand why the Dutch government cared so much, you need to know what was happening in the Netherlands in 1608. For forty years the northern Dutch provinces had been fighting for independence from the King of Spain, in a long struggle later called the Eighty Years' War. The Dutch army was led by Maurice of Nassau, Prince of Orange, one of the most skilled military commanders in Europe. He was famous for training his soldiers carefully and for using mathematics and engineering in war, so a clever new instrument was exactly the sort of thing that would interest him.

Think about what a spyglass meant in a world without radios, radar or airplanes. A general on a hill could study an enemy camp from a safe distance, count the tents and cannons, and see which way troops were moving. A lookout on a city wall could spot an approaching army sooner. At sea, the advantage was even bigger. A ship's captain who could recognize another ship's flags and guns before that ship could see him clearly had time to choose: attack, run, or prepare a defense. For a trading nation whose fleets sailed to Asia, Africa and the Americas, that extra warning could save cargoes worth fortunes and the lives of sailors.

In 1608 peace talks were going on in The Hague between the Dutch and representatives of Spain and its allies, and they led to a pause in the fighting, the Twelve Years' Truce, signed in April 1609. The Spanish side's commander, Ambrogio Spinola, was in The Hague for the talks. A newsletter from the time reported that Spinola was shown the new spyglass, and that he realized at once that it would make it harder for him to hide his own troops from the Dutch. Whether or not every word of that report is exact, it shows how quickly everyone understood the military meaning of the new tube.

This is also why governments were interested in controlling who could make telescopes. If only the Dutch army had them, it would have a real advantage. The trouble was that the device was simple, and secrets about simple devices do not stay secret for long. Within months, armies and navies all over Europe could buy one, and spyglasses became standard equipment for officers and ship captains for the next three hundred years.

sections.heading: News Travels Fast
paragraphs: In September 1608 something remarkable arrived in The Hague: an embassy, or official group of diplomats, sent by King Ekathotsarot of Siam, the country we now call Thailand. They had sailed from Asia on Dutch ships and reached The Hague on 10 September 1608. It is thought to have been the first embassy from Siam ever to visit Europe, and it caused a stir. The envoys met Prince Maurice, and a French-language newsletter was printed to describe their visit. Its title can be translated as 'Embassies of the King of Siam sent to His Excellency Prince Maurice.'

At the end of that newsletter, almost as an extra bit of news, was a paragraph about a spectacle maker from Middelburg who had made a device for seeing far. The newsletter claimed that with it one could see, from The Hague, the clock of the town of Delft and the church windows of Leiden, towns that were miles away. Because the newsletter was about a famous and unusual diplomatic visit, it was copied and passed around among educated people, diplomats and scholars across Europe. News of the telescope hitched a ride with news of the Siamese visitors.

Things moved fast after that. In November 1608 a copy of the report reached Paolo Sarpi in Venice. Sarpi was a monk, a scholar and an adviser to the Venetian government, and he was very interested in science. He began trying to learn more about the instrument and wrote to friends about it. Meanwhile, the spyglasses themselves were traveling. Craftsmen in other towns heard what was needed and began making their own, and traders carried Dutch-made ones to fairs and markets.

By April 1609, small three-power spyglasses were on sale in spectacle makers' shops on the Pont Neuf, a famous bridge in Paris lined with stalls. That was less than seven months after Lipperhey's letter. By the summer of 1609 spyglasses had reached several Italian cities, and they were also in London. In an age when a letter could take weeks to cross Europe on horseback, this was astonishing speed. It was one of the first times a new technology spread across a continent in about a single year.

Most people who bought these early spyglasses treated them as a curiosity or a handy gadget. Merchants used them to spot ships coming into port. Wealthy people showed them off to friends at parties. Soldiers took them to war. Very few people thought to aim them carefully at the night sky and write down what they saw. But a few did, and one of them was living just outside London.

sections.heading: Thomas Harriot's Moon
paragraphs: Thomas Harriot was one of the most brilliant English scientists of his time, but for centuries few people knew his name. Born around 1560, he studied at the University of Oxford, finishing his degree in 1580. As a young man he worked for the explorer Sir Walter Raleigh, and in 1585 and 1586 he joined an expedition to Roanoke Island, in what is now North Carolina, where he learned some of the Algonquian language spoken by the local people and wrote a famous report about the land. Later he was supported by a rich patron, Henry Percy, the Earl of Northumberland, and lived at Syon House, a grand house beside the river Thames just west of London.

Early in 1609 Harriot got hold of a Dutch spyglass, which the English sometimes called a 'Dutch trunke.' It magnified about six times. On the evening of 26 July 1609, by the old-style calendar still used in England (5 August 1609 by the calendar most of Europe used), he pointed it at the Moon, which was a thin crescent about five days old. Then he did something nobody is known to have done before: he made a drawing of what he saw.

Harriot's sketch is simple. It shows the curved bright edge of the crescent, the jagged line where light meets darkness, and a few dark patches. It is not a detailed map, and Harriot did not explain what the shapes meant. But it is the earliest known drawing of the Moon made through a telescope, made about four months before Galileo began his own famous Moon studies. Harriot kept observing. By 1610 and the following years he had drawn more detailed pictures, and by around 1613 he had made maps of the whole Moon with many craters placed correctly.

Harriot also shared spyglasses with friends. One of them, Sir William Lower, who lived in Wales, wrote to him in 1610 describing the Moon seen through his instrument. Lower compared its speckled look to a tart that his cook had made, with bright and dark spots all over it. It is a wonderfully ordinary comparison for an extraordinary sight, and it shows how strange the newly revealed Moon seemed to people who had always seen it as smooth.

Harriot's work went further. In December 1610 he recorded sunspots, dark marks on the Sun, which is the earliest record we have of anyone observing them through a telescope. Over the next few years he wrote down hundreds of sunspot observations. Yet he published almost none of it. Historians suggest several reasons. His patron, the Earl of Northumberland, had been locked in the Tower of London after the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, which may have made Harriot cautious. He may also have worried about being accused of having dangerous religious ideas. And he seems simply to have preferred working on problems to writing them up. Many of his papers were later lost or forgotten, and his telescope work was only properly recognized centuries later.

sections.heading: A Toy That Was About to Become a Tool
paragraphs: So by the summer of 1609, the telescope was already loose in the world. It had been described in a government letter, mentioned in a diplomatic newsletter, sold on a Paris bridge, carried to war, and aimed at least once at the Moon by an English mathematician. Yet in an important sense, the real story had barely begun.

Almost all of these spyglasses were weak, around three to six times. Their lenses were rough, their view was narrow, and the image wobbled whenever your hand shook. Nobody had yet worked out how to make them much stronger in a reliable way. And nobody had yet used one to make a series of careful observations, explain what they meant, and announce them to the world in print. The tube was a gadget. It had not yet become a scientific instrument.

That change needed a particular kind of person: someone who understood the mathematics of how lenses bend light, who had a workshop and skilled hands, who was patient enough to grind and test lens after lens, and who was bold enough to point the result at the heavens and argue about what he found. In 1609 such a person happened to be teaching mathematics at a university in northern Italy, close to Venice, where Paolo Sarpi was busy collecting every rumor he could about the Dutch device.
When the news of the Dutch tube reached this professor, he did not just buy one. He decided to build a better one.

deepDive: Historians of science such as Albert Van Helden have spent decades sorting through the surviving papers about the telescope's origins, and their conclusions are more interesting than a simple 'who was first' answer. The States General documents show two patent requests in October 1608, from Lipperhey on the 2nd and Metius on the 17th, plus signs that other craftsmen knew the trick. The Janssen claim rests mainly on testimony collected in 1655, decades later, from his son, whose dates contradict each other. Most scholars therefore treat the telescope as an invention that surfaced among Dutch lens makers in 1608, possibly more than once, rather than the work of a single lone genius. The physics explains why it was both easy and hard to discover. The magnification of this kind of telescope equals the objective's focal length divided by the eyepiece's focal length. Spectacle makers described lens strength by focal length too, so with an objective of about 30 cm and a concave eyepiece of about 10 cm you get about 3 times, while reaching 10 or 20 times needs a much weaker objective or a much stronger eyepiece than ordinary spectacle stock. That is one reason early instruments stalled at 3 to 6 times until someone ground special lenses. A second problem is lens quality. Glass of the period contained bubbles and streaks, and the curved surfaces were not perfectly spherical, so rays passing near the edge of a lens focused in the wrong place. Makers discovered that masking the objective down to a smaller opening, called stopping down the aperture, sharpened the image, at the cost of making it dimmer. The design also has a built-in limit: because the concave eyepiece spreads light out, the field of view is very narrow, a weakness that later designs would solve. Finally, the speed of the spread deserves attention. From a single letter in October 1608 to shops on the Pont Neuf by April 1609 and a telescopic Moon drawing in England by July 1609 (old style) took less than a year, carried by printed newsletters, diplomatic letters and traveling traders. It is an early example of how a cheap, easily copied technology can escape any attempt to keep it secret.
funFact: By April 1609, less than seven months after Lipperhey's patent letter, small spyglasses were already on sale in shops on the Pont Neuf bridge in Paris.
